cards.rueckseite:
**Imaging:** symmetric **vasogenic edema**, predominantly **parieto-occipital** subcortical white matter (watershed zones); brainstem/cerebellar variants exist. Hemorrhage (ICH/SAH) in up to **15%**, a few progress to infarction (restricted diffusion = worse prognosis).
**Clinic:** headache, seizures, encephalopathy, **cortical blindness**.
**Causes:** hypertensive crisis (~75% hypertensive), **(pre)eclampsia** (also 4–9 days postpartum), sepsis, autoimmune disease, **cyclosporine/tacrolimus**, chemotherapy, transplantation.
**Treatment:** control BP, remove the cause (stop drug, deliver placenta).

Hypometabolism/hypoperfusion of the **cerebellar hemisphere contralateral** to a supratentorial lesion (stroke, tumor), from interruption of the **cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathway**. Seen on PET/SPECT/perfusion imaging; not a second lesion.

zeilen: Tremor, anxiety, insomnia, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea
Generalized tonic-clonic, usually early and brief
Confusion, hallucinations, marked autonomic hyperactivity, fever; potentially fatal
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 212–214. Treatment: benzodiazepines (symptom-triggered, e.g., CIWA-Ar), thiamine before glucose; β-blockers/clonidine only as adjuncts because they mask withdrawal.

cards.text: Chronic alcohol abuse causes cerebellar degeneration from loss of {{c1::Purkinje cells}}, mainly in the {{c2::anterior superior vermis}}, producing a {{c3::wide-based gait ataxia with relatively spared limb coordination}}.

cards.vorderseite: Acute transverse myelitis: definition and first step
cards.rueckseite:
Inflammatory spinal cord syndrome (sensory level, paraparesis, bladder dysfunction) over hours to weeks. **Myelitis** = inflammatory; **myelopathy** = compressive, toxic or metabolic.
**First step:** urgent **MRI** to exclude a **compressive lesion** (surgical emergency).
Causes: postinfectious/viral, MS, **NMO (AQP4)**, MOG, SLE/Sjögren, sarcoid, paraneoplastic, radiation, decompression sickness, idiopathic.
Work-up: LP (pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands), AQP4/MOG antibodies, brain MRI.

CNS involvement in ≈ 5% of sarcoidosis; only 1–3% isolated to the CNS.
**Most common neurologic manifestation:** **diabetes insipidus** (hypothalamus).
Also **multiple cranial nerve palsies** (facial nerve most common, often bilateral), basal granulomatous meningitis, hydrocephalus, intramedullary lesions.
Pathology: **noncaseating granulomas**. Labs: ACE in serum/CSF (low sensitivity).
Treatment: corticosteroids, other immunosuppressants.

For prior reactions (even hives):
- **Prednisone 50 mg PO** three times before the study (Greenberg: 20–24 h, 8–12 h and 2 h before; ACR: 13, 7 and 1 h)
- **Diphenhydramine 50 mg** IM 1 h or IV 5 min before
- ± H2 blocker; use **non-ionic** contrast
- Emergency: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, scan within 2 h

After previous anaphylaxis/airway edema: avoid iodinated contrast unless essential. The same prep is used for gadolinium allergy.

cards.text: **Metformin** and iodinated contrast: hold metformin {{c1::48 h}} before and after contrast (and ≈ 48 h before surgery) because of the risk of {{c2::lactic acidosis}} if contrast-induced renal failure delays its excretion.

cards.vorderseite: Inadvertent intrathecal injection of non-approved (ionic) contrast
cards.rueckseite:
Causes refractory seizures, myoclonus, cerebral edema, ICH, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, coma, death.
**Management:**
- Immediately withdraw CSF + contrast through the needle
- **Head up ≈ 45°** (keep contrast out of the head)
- Airway, **antiseizure drugs** (often several), sedation/paralysis, cooling
- IV steroids, antihistamine, hydration, BP control
- **Lumbar drain** with CSF drainage (≈ 10 mL/h)
- Monitor CK, electrolytes, EEG

Only agent approved for intrathecal use: **iohexol (Omnipaque)**.

Fibrosis of skin, joints and organs in **severe renal failure** (mostly dialysis patients); risk ≈ 2.4% per contrast MRI in end-stage renal disease.
- GFR **30–60:** relative contraindication
- GFR **< 30:** contraindicated
- **Macrocyclic** agents (Dotarem, Gadovist, ProHance) are safest; **linear** agents (Omniscan, Magnevist) carry higher NSF risk and more gadolinium retention in the brain.

Pregnancy: gadolinium contraindicated throughout.

- Pacemaker/ICD, neurostimulators, cochlear implants, infusion pumps (unless MR-conditional)
- **Ferromagnetic aneurysm clips** (clips made **after 1990** are non-ferromagnetic)
- **Metal fragments in the eye**, shrapnel/BBs
- Pulmonary artery catheter
- Vascular stent, coil or filter placed within the last **6 weeks**
- Relative: claustrophobia, critically ill, obesity
- **Programmable shunt valve:** usually tolerates 3 T, but the **setting can change → recheck after every MRI**

cards.text: Fetal radiation risk is highest during the {{c1::first 2 weeks after conception}} (miscarriage) and at {{c2::8–16 weeks of gestation}} (cognitive disability). Head or C-spine CT gives the fetus only a {{c3::small dose that shielding reduces further}}; abdominal CT exposes it directly.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Gray (Gy):** absorbed dose, 1 J/kg = 100 rad
- **Sievert (Sv):** dose equivalent = Gy × quality factor (X-rays Q = 1) = 100 rem
- 1 rem ≈ 300 extra cancers per million people
- Average annual exposure ≈ **360 mrem (3.6 mSv)**; transcontinental flight ≈ 5 mrem; chest X-ray 10–40 mrem

Effects: **deterministic** (threshold, e.g., cataract, skin burn) vs. **stochastic** (any dose raises risk, e.g., leukemia). Protect with time, distance, shielding; keep hands out of the primary beam.

- **Burst suppression:** bursts alternating with flat periods; barbiturate/propofol coma target, severe anoxia
- **Periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges (PLEDs/LPDs):** acute focal lesion (stroke, tumor, abscess), **HSV encephalitis** (temporal)
- **Periodic sharp waves 1–2 Hz:** **Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease** (reactive to stimuli, unlike most PLEDs)
- **Triphasic waves:** nonspecific; hepatic/metabolic encephalopathy, post-anoxia
- **3 Hz spike-and-wave:** absence seizures; **hypsarrhythmia:** West syndrome
- **Electrocerebral silence:** supports brain death (ancillary)

cards.text: Intraoperative SSEP warning criteria: amplitude drop of {{c1::≥ 50%}} or latency increase of {{c2::> 10%}}. For transcranial MEPs, a {{c3::sustained 50% (or greater) amplitude loss}} is significant. SSEPs are averaged, so they lag behind acute injury and monitor only the {{c4::dorsal columns}}.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Volatile agents and N₂O** depress cortical SSEP amplitude and, even more, **MEPs** (dose-dependent) → use **TIVA** (propofol + opioid)
- **Neuromuscular blockade** abolishes MEPs and free-running EMG (SSEPs unaffected)
- Opioids have minimal effect
- Also check hypotension, hypothermia, anemia and limb position before blaming the surgery
- BAERs are very resistant to anesthetics

cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 14.4, p. 251. Prolonged I–V interpeak latency suggests a retrocochlear lesion such as vestibular schwannoma; loss of wave V during CPA surgery warns of hearing loss.

cards.text: SSEP generators (median nerve): {{c1::N9 (Erb's point)}} = brachial plexus, {{c2::N13}} = cervicomedullary junction/dorsal horn, {{c3::N19/N20}} = primary somatosensory cortex. Posterior tibial nerve: cortical peak {{c4::P37–P40}}.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves:** appear ≈ **3 weeks** after denervation (earliest 7–10 days, sometimes 3–4 weeks) → EMG too early is falsely normal
- Increased insertional activity (more ACh receptors)
- **Reinnervation:** polyphasic MUAPs (> 4 phases) from ≈ 6–8 weeks, mostly after 3–6 months; later large, long-duration motor units with reduced recruitment
- Fasciculations: nonspecific, typical for ALS; "dive bomber" discharges: myotonia

- **F-wave:** antidromic stimulation of anterior horn cells that then fire back orthodromically; tests **proximal motor conduction** → prolonged/absent early in **Guillain–Barré**
- **H-reflex:** electrical analog of the **ankle jerk**, monosynaptic Ia reflex, practical only for **S1** → lost in S1 radiculopathy
- **SNAP:** preserved in **preganglionic** lesions (root, avulsion) because the dorsal root ganglion lies in the foramen; reduced in postganglionic (plexus, nerve) lesions

cards.text: Post-LP headache: typically starts {{c1::24–48 h}} after the puncture, is {{c2::worse upright and relieved lying down}}, lasts a mean of {{c3::4 days}}, and occurs in about {{c4::20%}} (more in young women, with larger or cutting needles). Treatment if persistent: {{c5::epidural blood patch}}.

Normal **prevertebral soft tissue** on lateral C-spine imaging (adult, classic rule): ≤ {{c1::7 mm at C2}} and ≤ {{c2::22 mm at C6}}. Sensitivity for injury is low (≈ 60% at C3), and an {{c3::endotracheal tube}} or facial/skull base fractures can cause false widening.
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 12.2, p. 224 (values differ slightly for MDCT)
